niche_preference_profile: This user most consistently prefers interfaces with clear hierarchy, readable structure, and explicit affordances. They often favor light or mixed-light layouts with neutral surfaces and restrained purple/pink accents, though in some task-heavy or immersive dark UIs they prefer cleaner dark themes over cluttered alternatives. They like spacious layouts when it improves clarity, but they also accept compact dense rows in data-heavy views when that increases scanability and organization. They prefer grouped lists/cards over fragmented layouts, visible labels and helper text, explicit status indicators, rounded softer components, and primary actions that are clearly prioritized without excessive visual noise.

top_7_criteria.description: Prefers strong visual hierarchy with clear section titles, grouped content, readable structure, explicit labels, and obvious separation between primary and secondary information.

Usually prefers light neutral backgrounds, soft gray surfaces, and restrained accent colors such as purple, pink, or muted blue; generally rejects overly dark, high-contrast, or aggressively saturated palettes unless the dark option is cleaner and more focused.
Prefers layouts that are easy to scan: spacious and breathable in general-purpose flows, but compact and information-efficient in list or analytics views when rows remain organized and legible.
Prefers unified cards, grouped rows, integrated bottom sheets, and clearly organized sections over fragmented cards, detached full pages, split panels, or scattered competing elements.

Prefers actions that are explicit and understandable, with visible buttons, text labels, clear selected states, and a dominant primary action when needed; rejects hidden, icon-only, or weakly signaled controls.
Prefers softer rounded shapes, subtle shadows, restrained depth, muted controls, and a calm minimalist presentation over harsh, decorative, overly heavy, or visually noisy styling.

Prefers interfaces that provide visible helper text, examples, numbered ordering, verbal status labels, selected-state feedback, and other direct guidance rather than relying on implicit or purely visual cues.
